title: Nib and the Giggle-Mites
markdown:
On the tippy-top of the Crumbling Peaks, where the wind hummed and the ledges pretended they were meant for walking, lived a clever little goblin named Nib and his best friend, a shaggy loyal goat kid called Biscuit.

Nib had moss-green skin and eyes that sparkled with a curiosity you do not see every day. He was a tinkerer. His cave stuffed itself with contraptions of twigs, vines, and shiny mountain rock. His latest big idea: find the legendary Whispering Moss, said to glow with captured moonlight even at noon, growing only on the highest windiest ledges where eagles dared to nest.

“Come on, Biscuit!” He tugged his worn leather satchel. Biscuit, fur like a well-loved sheepskin, mischievous twinkle, excited bleat, little beard wiggling. More than a pet: shadow, confidante, sometimes the quiet voice of sense. Nib had found him years ago, a tiny lost kid shivering near a roaring waterfall. Inseparable since. Biscuit was a marvel on tricky paths; his head-butts cleared the prickliest brambles.

The search led them to the Whispering Gorge, a deep dark chasm so wide you could barely see the other side. A bridge that looked held together by wishes spanned the gap. Guarding it, arms solid as a landslide: Grok the Ogre. Not mean. Official. He loved rules, adored order, and oh, how he loved forms — especially ones that needed signing, stamping, and notarising.

“Halt,” rumbled Grok, pebbles tumbling down a slope. “No one crosses without proper authorisation. A matter of utmost importance.”

Nib blinked. “Authorisation? To cross a bridge, sir?”

“Indeed.” Chest puffed. “Form G-7B, Application for Trans-Mountain Transit, in triplicate. With the supplementary affidavit for Caprine Companions, naturally.” A surprisingly gentle heave produced a stack of parchment that nearly tickled Nib’s nose.

Nib stared. Biscuit nudged his leg, as if to say a goat kid needed a special form. “Sir, there are no other bridges for miles. I’m only looking for a special herb.”

“Rules are rules, little goblin.” Grok’s brow furrowed. He truly thought this made perfect sense.

Nib sighed. Sticky situation; clever brain required. Satchel: foraging knife, vine-rope, magnifying glass for tiny leaves, a half-eaten mushroom pastry smelling delightfully earthy. No ink. No quill. No sliver of patience for a ridiculously long form.

Just as he wondered whether pastry could serve as a pen, a peculiar sound drifted through the gorge. A faint tinkling giggle, tiny bells of dew. Then another. A shimmering swarm of iridescent insects, no bigger than fireflies, zipped past Nib’s nose and buzzed around Grok’s impressive ears until the ogre winced.

“Botheration and fiddle-sticks. The Giggle-Mites are back. They always show up when the mist is thick. Last week they tickled Mayor Grumbles so much he declared Tuesday National Fuzzball Day. A complete bureaucratic nightmare.”

Nib’s eyes lit. He had heard tales. Mischievous sprites, drawn to strong emotions — especially frustration and paperwork in triplicate.

“Grok. Perhaps I can assist with your Giggle-Mite situation.”

Grok eyed the small goblin. “And what do goblins know of pest control, besides riddles or particularly smelly cheese?”

“Giggle-Mites detest good cheer,” Nib said, grin wide, “and they adore silly nonsensical paperwork. If I coax them away from your bridge and your forms, your administrative duties might be a little less ticklish.”

Biscuit, sensing a plan, nudged the enormous stack. A few sheets fluttered. The mites, attracted by fluttering paper and Nib’s cheerful anticipation, swarmed the parchment. Nib flicked a handful of sticky sweet mountain berries toward dense firs beneath a crumbling ancient tower, mist swirling like a ghostly scarf. The mites, captivated by sugary scent and jiggling flight, followed obediently into the woods.

Grok’s jaw nearly hit dusty ground. Tinkling grew fainter, gone. “Well, I’ll be a turnip. Vanished.” He looked at Nib, then at Biscuit, who was happily nibbling a stray corner of parchment. “You actually solved it. Without a single ink stain.”

Nib had another idea. “About that form. Since I’ve assisted with your administrative pest problem, perhaps you could overlook the triplicate for my little herb-gathering expedition?”

Grok scratched his enormous chin. “The rulebook does state, section 4, subsection C, that assistance in mitigating inter-species administrative annoyance may be grounds for expedited processing and reduced paperwork.” He squinted, flipping pages with a surprisingly delicate touch. “And you did mitigate. Quite effectively.” A dramatic flourish: he tore off the top sheet. “Just this one. First page. Sign the bottom. For my official records.”

Nib beamed, his heart swelling with delight. He quickly scribbled his name and today's date. Biscuit added an enthusiastic hoof-print smudge that looked remarkably like a tiny happy mountain. Grok stamped with a giant slightly muddy thumbprint, which somehow looked perfectly official.

“Right then.” A smile tugged. “You may pass. And if you see any more Giggle-Mites on your way back, send them my way. I have a tedious decree about the proper sizing of turnips that is desperately in need of filing. I suspect they might speed things up.”

Nib and Biscuit waved, satchel lighter, hearts lighter. They had not found the Whispering Moss today. They had found a one-page form, a fair ogre, and a goat who had improved official records with a hoof. The moss could wait on its windy ledge. The gorge, for the moment, had stopped asking for triplicate, which was a kind of moonlight of its own. They ambled the winding paths as the sun dipped, orange and purple on the jagged peaks, pine and damp earth in their lungs, Biscuit’s head under Nib’s palm, the Crumbling Peaks already inventing the next sticky situation and, with any luck, the next swarm.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
